metadataFromPriorUpload.title: Somatic vs Germ-Line Mutations, and Coding vs Non-Coding DNA | Year 12 Biology Module 6
metadataFromPriorUpload.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module6/lesson05

The same BRCA1 mutation can be in every cell of your body, or in just one. Why can only one of those be inherited? See how a somatic mutation spreads into a patch of cells by mitosis and can start a cancer, how a germ-line mutation ends up in every cell of the next generation, why only 1 to 2 per cent of our DNA codes for protein, and how a change in non-coding DNA, like the one behind lactase persistence, can still change what a gene does. Two exam-style questions with brief feedback.

0:29 Two places a mutation can happen
0:47 Somatic mutations
1:18 Germ-line mutations

2:15 Coding DNA

3:41 Introns

4:53 Memory

6:55 Answer 2
7:20 Decision rule
7:46 Key notes

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 6, Genetic Change. Inquiry question: "How does mutation introduce new alleles into a population?"
Syllabus dotpoints (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 6):
"distinguish between somatic mutations and germ-line mutations and their effect on an organism   (ACSBL082, ACSBL083)"
"assess the significance of ‘coding’ and ‘non-coding’ DNA segments in the process of mutation (ACSBL078)"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: What changes when chromosomes mutate. Next: Mutation practice: HSC-style questions.
